strengths: Significance: Syndrome-dependent reweighting of MWPM is a useful direction for quantum error correction. Retaining a combinatorial decoder while learning contextual edge scores offers a plausible way to improve on static geometric weights.

Empirical merits: Figures 2–4 report improvements over MWPM and BPOSD-2 across several toric-code sizes and competitive performance against QECCT on rotated surface codes. Evaluating two geometries and both independent and depolarizing noise provides useful initial evidence.

Presentation and reproducibility: The paper clearly outlines the prediction-and-matching pipeline and supplies substantial architectural detail. Appendix B specifies the optimizer, learning-rate schedule, batch size, layer counts, entropy coefficient, and GPU. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the reported simulation study.
weaknesses: Soundness—logical equivalence and correction construction: Section 3.3 incorrectly states that errors producing identical syndromes are logically equivalent; they can differ by a nontrivial logical operator. This distinction matters directly to the proposed supervision. A defect pairing alone does not specify the physical correction or its homology class, yet the manuscript does not adequately explain path selection, periodic wrapping, or logical-observable tracking when converting predicted matchings into corrections. Section 4.2 even defines toric distances using ordinary Manhattan distance without describing periodic adjustment. These omissions prevent verification of the central decoding procedure.

Soundness—training-label construction: Algorithm 2 leaves FindValidPermutation unspecified, and the timed brute-force fallback has no search budget, failure rate, or timeout policy. Permuting endpoint pairings alone is not guaranteed to recover a correction in the desired logical class, particularly for configurations containing nontrivial closed loops. The claim that a valid ground truth is ensured therefore requires qualification and evidence. It is also unclear whether unsuccessful label generation filters the training distribution.

Soundness—statistical evidence: The manuscript does not report test-shot counts, logical-failure counts, training-seed variability, or an explained uncertainty-estimation procedure. Figure 4 gives precise thresholds of 10.95% and 17.9% without a finite-size scaling fit, confidence intervals, or systematic-error analysis. With distances only up to 10, the claimed near-optimal threshold and the 17.9% versus 17.8% advantage over QECCT are not convincingly established.

Originality and attribution: The architecture combines established graph attention, Transformer, and matching components, while the proposed proxy objective is supervised BCE plus entropy minimization. This may be a useful engineering contribution, but it does not differentiate through MWPM or directly optimize logical failure, making the claims of novel end-to-end optimization overstated. No ablations isolate the GNN, global attention, entropy penalty, or label-generation strategy. Probability polarization in Figure 5 is expected under entropy minimization and does not independently demonstrate improved decoding.

Significance and scalability: Section 5.4 acknowledges attention cost quadratic in the number of defect-pair edges. For D defects, the complete graph has O(D²) edges, yielding O(D⁴) attention cost; at fixed nonzero noise density, this can scale as O(L⁸). Approximately constant parameter count therefore does not establish manageable runtime or activation memory. No latency, peak-memory, training-time, or larger-distance measurements support the claims of superior scalability and viability at larger code distances.

Reproducibility and presentation: The graph is described as complete over active defects, but preprocessing includes all stabilizers and the complexity discussion assumes sparse GNN connectivity; the actual message-passing graph is unclear. Rotated-code boundary handling at inference and positional encoding are insufficiently specified. Training spans 200–1000 epochs without per-experiment budgets or selection criteria, and baseline training/tuning details and an implementation-release statement are absent.

Evaluation scope and limitations: The experiments cover small codes with idealized data-qubit noise, without repeated noisy syndrome measurements or circuit-level faults. This is a legitimate initial scope, but the conclusion does not adequately limit its fault-tolerance and scalability claims. Correlation-aware matching baselines are also missing despite exploiting noise correlations being a central motivation. Together with the unresolved methodological and statistical issues, these gaps outweigh the promising reported gains.

strengths: Significance: Syndrome-dependent reweighting of MWPM addresses a useful problem: exploiting error correlations while retaining a classical matching decoder. The reported reductions in logical error rate, particularly for the distance-10 toric code under depolarizing noise, merit further investigation.

Empirical merits: The evaluation includes two code geometries, multiple distances, two noise models, and comparisons with MWPM, BPOSD-2, and QECCT. The manuscript appropriately acknowledges parity with QECCT for the distance-7 rotated surface code.

Presentation and reproducibility: The overall pipeline is understandable, and the manuscript provides architecture equations, pseudocode, optimizer settings, learning-rate schedule, and hardware information. These offer a useful starting point for implementation.
weaknesses: Soundness—training-label validity is unresolved. Section 4.4 calls labels optimal correction chains but constructs them using a heuristic, matching permutations, and timed brute-force search. It does not specify timeout handling, failure rates, or whether unsuccessful samples are excluded. Endpoint pairings alone do not specify a correction's homology: different paths between the same defects can differ by a logical operator, and a noncontractible closed error loop has no endpoints. The manuscript needs to explain path selection and unrepresentable cases before claiming that this procedure ensures valid ground truth.

Soundness—threshold claims exceed the evidence. Figure 4 reports thresholds of 10.95% and 17.9%, including a small advantage over QECCT's 17.8%, without test-shot counts, confidence intervals, repeated-training variability, or a finite-size scaling procedure. The small tested distances and plotted crossings do not establish this precision or the claimed proximity to maximum-likelihood performance. Baseline threshold lines are shown without the corresponding size-dependent curves needed to assess their estimation.

Soundness and originality—the proposed mechanism is not isolated. There are no ablations removing the GNN, Transformer, entropy penalty, or specialized label construction. Consequently, attributing improvements to local/global processing or describing entropy regularization as critical is unsupported. BCE plus entropy minimization is a conventional supervised surrogate; it does not differentiate through MWPM or directly optimize logical failure. The claims of a novel loss and end-to-end optimization need qualification, and the specific advance over prior neural reweighting or hybrid decoding approaches needs clearer positioning.

Significance—scalability is overstated. For m active defects, a complete graph has O(m²) edges, so dense attention over edge tokens incurs O(m⁴) attention cost. Nearly constant parameter count therefore does not establish manageable inference memory or runtime. Sections 5.5 and 7 claim viability at larger distances and superior scalability without latency, peak-memory, throughput, or larger-distance measurements. Section 5.4 also invokes sparse GNN connectivity without reconciling it with the complete graph described earlier.

Reproducibility—important implementation choices remain unspecified. The manuscript does not clearly define the GNN adjacency over active and inactive stabilizers, restrictions on matching different stabilizer types, inference-time boundary-node construction, or conversion of matched pairs into physical correction paths. The stated Manhattan distance omits periodic wrapping for the toric code. Appendix B gives a broad 200–1000 epoch range without per-experiment settings, and baseline tuning and training budgets are insufficiently documented.

Presentation—several explanations are technically misleading. Section 3.3 states that errors producing identical syndromes are logically equivalent; this holds only when their difference is a stabilizer, not a nontrivial logical operator. Section 6 treats polarized probabilities as evidence of successful decoding, although entropy minimization explicitly encourages polarization and confidence alone does not establish correctness. These issues affect the central motivation and interpretation, rather than merely wording.

Limitations and ethics: No material research-ethics concern is apparent. However, the conclusions insufficiently qualify the restriction to small codes and idealized noise without measurement faults, the unresolved label-generation failures, and the absence of runtime evidence. These limitations constrain the practical claims; the decisive reason for rejection is the unsupported correctness and performance claims, not the specialized scope itself.

strengths: Significance: Learning syndrome-dependent weights while retaining MWPM is a useful approach to improving quantum error correction. Figures 2–3 report gains over MWPM and BPOSD-2 across two code geometries, with particularly promising improvements for the distance-10 toric code.
Originality: The combination of edge-level neural prediction, classical matching, and simulation-derived matching supervision provides a concrete hybrid decoder design worth investigating.

Presentation and reproducibility: The paper clearly outlines the inference pipeline and provides architecture equations, pseudocode, optimizer settings, and hardware information. Comparison with QECCT helps contextualize the empirical contribution.
weaknesses: Soundness—training-label construction: Section 4.4 leaves the central supervision procedure insufficiently specified. FindValidPermutation, the timed brute-force fallback, timeout handling, and failure rates are not described. A matching of defect endpoints does not by itself specify the physical correction path or its homology class. The manuscript must explain path selection, periodic wrapping, and boundary handling, and establish when a logically valid target is representable. Section 3.3 also incorrectly states that errors with identical syndromes are necessarily logically equivalent; they can differ by a logical operator.

Soundness—statistical evidence: No evaluation shot counts, uncertainty intervals, repeated-run variability, or threshold-fitting procedure are reported. Consequently, the claimed threshold advantages of 17.9% versus 17.8% and the precise 10.95% independent-noise threshold are not adequately supported by Figure 4 and the small code distances evaluated. The curves suggest improvement, but do not establish these precise asymptotic claims.

Soundness and originality—objective and attribution: Equation 26 uses supervised BCE plus entropy minimization; it does not differentiate through MWPM or directly optimize logical decoding success. Describing this as a novel end-to-end solution to the combinatorial optimization barrier overstates what is demonstrated. No ablations isolate the GNN, global Transformer, entropy penalty, or labeling heuristic. Figure 5's increased confidence is encouraged by the loss itself and does not establish improved correctness or explain the observed gains.

Significance—unsupported scalability claims: For D active defects, the complete candidate graph has O(D²) edges, so dense attention over edge tokens costs O(D⁴) at fixed hidden dimension. At fixed physical noise rate, D grows with lattice area. Approximately constant parameter counts therefore do not establish manageable inference memory or runtime. No latency, peak-memory, or larger-distance measurements support the strong scalability conclusions in Sections 5.5 and 7.

Reproducibility and presentation: The graph specification alternates between a complete active-defect graph, features for all stabilizers, and sparse local GNN connectivity without defining their relationship. Cross-type matching restrictions and inference-time virtual-node construction are unclear. The stated toric distance omits periodic wrapping. Appendix B gives a broad 200–1000 epoch range without per-experiment settings, and baseline tuning, evaluation sampling, and code availability are not documented.

Limitations and ethics: The experiments provide useful evidence for small codes under independent and depolarizing data-qubit noise, but do not establish performance with noisy syndrome measurements, circuit-level noise, or transfer to unseen distances. These boundaries need explicit treatment rather than broad claims of generalization and practical scalability. No material research-ethics concern is apparent; the recommendation is driven by methodological and evidential gaps.

strengths: Significance: Syndrome-dependent weighting of a classical matching decoder is a useful direction. Figure 2 reports consistent improvements over standard and correlated MWPM across several toric and rotated-code distances, with additional comparisons against QECCT and BPOSD-2.
Originality: The combination of graph-based node processing, attention over candidate matching edges, and logically verified matching-label construction provides a concrete hybrid decoding approach.

Presentation and reproducibility: The pipeline, training objective, and label-generation procedure are described through equations and pseudocode. Appendix B supplies major architectural and optimization settings, and Appendix G reports measured inference times.

The manuscript transparently reports training-data filtering and explicitly states that evaluation samples are never discarded. Its impact statement appropriately acknowledges quantum computing's cryptographic implications; no material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—threshold evidence: The central thresholds of 17.9%, 17.7%, and 10.95% lack a documented fitting procedure, finite-size scaling analysis, confidence intervals, or evaluation sample counts. Figure 2 uses small code distances, and uncertainty across training runs is also absent. Consequently, the claimed 17.9% versus 17.8% advantage over QECCT and near-optimal independent-noise threshold are not established at the reported precision.

Soundness—matching construction: Important details needed to obtain valid corrections are unresolved. Appendix D adds one ordinary virtual boundary node connected to all defects, but a perfect matching can use that node only once, whereas multiple defects may need boundary corrections. The manuscript must explain any special boundary semantics or node duplication. It also does not adequately specify restrictions between stabilizer types or how matched endpoints determine physical paths and their homology on the torus.

Scalability claims exceed the evidence. Section 4 constructs a complete defect graph, whereas Section 5.3 invokes sparse connectivity. With m defects, there are O(m²) edge tokens and dense edge attention costs O(m⁴), potentially O(Lcode⁸) at fixed noise density. Nearly constant parameter counts do not establish manageable activation memory or large-distance scalability. Timing at only distances 6 and 10, without a classical MWPM timing comparison or detailed benchmark protocol, does not resolve this limitation.

Originality and methodological justification: Equation 18 is supervised BCE plus entropy regularization; it does not differentiate through matching or directly optimize logical failure. Thus, claims of a novel end-to-end solution to MWPM's differentiation barrier are overstated. Labels are the first logically valid matchings found by a heuristic, rather than demonstrated optimal targets. The relationship between these edge marginals, the negative-log weighting rule, and logical-class decoding accuracy needs stronger justification.

Reproducibility remains inadequate despite the architectural detail. Evaluation shot counts, random seeds, model-selection procedures, per-configuration training durations, baseline settings, and circuit-level noise instructions are missing. The source-code reference supplies no usable repository URL. These omissions materially hinder verification of the small reported gains and reproduction of the circuit-noise experiments.

The analyses do not substantiate several explanatory claims. Ablations are restricted to toric distance 4 and do not separately establish the benefit of the GNN. The transfer experiment lacks a randomly initialized model trained for the same 20 epochs, so it cannot demonstrate accelerated adaptation. Separately training on different geometries and noise models also does not establish transfer across those settings. Circuit-level surface-code evidence is limited to distance 3 and three rounds.

Presentation contains a consequential conceptual error: Section 3.3 states that errors with identical syndromes are logically equivalent, although they can differ by a nontrivial logical operator. The abstract also attributes both quoted thresholds to depolarizing noise, whereas 10.95% concerns independent noise. Together with insufficient qualification of scalability and generalization claims, these issues require substantive revision before the contribution can be reliably built upon.

strengths: Significance: Syndrome-dependent reweighting of MWPM is a useful direction for quantum error correction, combining learned correlations with a structured classical decoder. Figure 2 reports consistent improvements over standard MWPM across toric and rotated surface codes, with comparisons to QECCT, BPOSD-2, and correlated MWPM.

Originality: The particular combination of graph processing, edge-level attention, and error-informed matching-label generation offers a potentially useful methodological contribution, even though its individual components are established.

Presentation and reproducibility: The pipeline is organized clearly, with architectural equations, training hyperparameters, and supplementary implementation details. Appendix G provides actual runtime measurements: 4.01 ms for NMWPM versus 20.1 ms for QECCT at toric distance 10 on the stated hardware.

Limitations and ethics: Appendix C transparently describes label-generation timeouts and training-data filtering, explicitly stating that evaluation samples are not discarded. The impact statement reasonably addresses quantum computing's cryptographic implications; I see no material ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness—threshold claims lack adequate statistical support. The headline thresholds of 17.9%, 10.95%, and 17.7% are presented without evaluation sample counts, confidence intervals, a specified threshold-estimation procedure, or finite-size scaling analysis. Figure 2 uses only small code distances, and the 17.9% versus 17.8% advantage over QECCT is particularly difficult to assess without uncertainty estimates. The reported curves support promising finite-size performance, but do not establish the claimed threshold precision or near-optimality.

Soundness and reproducibility—the conversion from a predicted matching to a physical correction is underspecified. Pairing defect endpoints does not uniquely determine a correction's homology on a torus. The paper does not explain path selection, periodic wraparound handling, or whether alternative homology classes for the same endpoint pair are represented. Section 4.2 defines distance using ordinary Manhattan coordinates despite periodic boundaries. Appendix D introduces a single virtual boundary node without explaining how multiple defects can independently terminate at boundaries under the stated perfect-matching constraint. These details are essential to reproduce both the labels and logical-error measurements.

Soundness and originality—the training objective is overstated. Equation 18 is supervised BCE with entropy regularization; it neither differentiates through MWPM nor directly optimizes logical decoding success. Appendix C selects the first valid matching, which is not necessarily an optimal or unique target. No analysis establishes that predicting these selected edge labels, followed by maximum symmetrization and negative-log weighting, recovers the most likely logical class. This heuristic can still be useful empirically, but the claims of resolving end-to-end optimization and predicting optimal weights require qualification.

Significance—large-scale efficiency is not demonstrated. With m active defects, a complete graph has O(m²) edges, making dense attention over edge tokens O(m⁴). Section 5.3 acknowledges quadratic attention in edge count, yet Sections 5.4 and 7 infer scalability from nearly constant parameter counts and small-distance results. Appendix G's useful two-distance timing comparison does not resolve activation-memory growth, noise-dependent runtime, or performance relative to standalone optimized MWPM. Its batching and timing protocol are also unspecified.

Evaluation and reproducibility remain incomplete. The manuscript omits test-shot counts, repeated-training variability, precise per-experiment training schedules within the stated 200–1000 epoch range, and sufficient baseline configuration details. The circuit-level experiments cover repetition distances 3 and 5 and a rotated surface code of distance 3, without fully specifying the circuit-noise configuration or the adaptation of features and labels to spacetime decoding. These experiments provide preliminary evidence, not broad validation under realistic noise.

Mechanistic and generalization claims exceed the controls. The ablation at distance 4 replaces the Transformer with an MLP but does not separately establish the GNN's necessity or the claimed local/global division, especially since the graph is described as complete. The transfer experiment compares a fine-tuned transferred model only against MWPM, not an equally trained model initialized from scratch. Evaluation using separately trained models on several geometries likewise does not establish cross-topology transfer.

Presentation contains consequential conceptual inaccuracies. Section 3.3 states that errors with identical syndromes are logically equivalent; they can instead differ by a nontrivial logical operator. The abstract also attributes both reported toric thresholds to depolarizing noise, although 10.95% concerns independent noise. These inaccuracies affect the interpretation of the central task and results.

strengths: Significance: Learning syndrome-dependent edge weights while retaining a classical matching decoder is a useful approach to exploiting error correlations. Figure 2 reports consistent logical-error-rate improvements across toric and rotated surface codes, with comparisons against MWPM, correlated MWPM, BPOSD-2, and QECCT.

Originality: The combination of error-configuration-derived matching labels, graph processing, and global attention over candidate edges provides a concrete hybrid decoding contribution, even though its individual components are established.

Presentation and reproducibility: The pipeline is organized clearly, with inference and label-generation pseudocode, architectural equations, training hyperparameters, and hardware information. Appendix C transparently reports training-data filtering and explicitly states that evaluation samples are never discarded.

The evaluation includes feature and loss ablations, limited noise-rate extrapolation, transfer experiments, and circuit-noise demonstrations. The impact statement appropriately acknowledges cryptographic implications; no material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—threshold evidence: The headline thresholds of 17.9% and 10.95% lack a documented finite-size fitting procedure, uncertainty estimates, evaluation sample counts, or variation across training seeds. Figure 2 uses small code distances, and the claimed advantage over QECCT of 17.9% versus 17.8% cannot be assessed statistically. The evidence supports promising finite-size performance, but not the precision or superiority of the threshold claims.

Soundness and reproducibility—matching semantics: Essential details are unresolved. The complete graph includes both stabilizer types, but the manuscript does not specify how incompatible cross-type matches are excluded. Appendix D introduces one virtual boundary node, whereas ordinary perfect matching permits that node to match only once; supporting multiple boundary terminations requires additional semantics. The conversion from matched endpoints to physical correction paths, including toric wrapping and path ties, is also unspecified. These details directly determine logical correctness.

Significance—scalability claims exceed the evidence: Section 5.3 acknowledges dense attention over all candidate edges. With m defects, a complete graph has O(m²) edges, implying O(m⁴) attention cost and, at fixed physical noise rate, potentially O(Lcode⁸) scaling. Nearly constant parameter counts do not establish manageable activation memory. Appendix G measures only distances 6 and 10, omits a classical MWPM timing baseline, and does not specify batching or noise rate. These results do not substantiate the broad claims of superior scalability.

Originality and methodological framing: Equation 18 is supervised BCE with entropy regularization; it neither differentiates through MWPM nor directly optimizes logical decoding success. Calling this a novel end-to-end optimization solution overstates what is established. Heuristic matching labels are valid corrections for sampled errors, but are not necessarily optimal or unique syndrome-conditioned targets. Section 3.3 also incorrectly states that errors with identical syndromes are necessarily logically equivalent.

Experimental attribution and generalization: The main ablations use only distance 4 and do not separately establish the necessity of the GNN and global Transformer at larger distances. Transfer from distance 10 to 8 is compared with MWPM rather than a model trained from scratch for the same 20 epochs. Consequently, the claimed benefit of transferred representations is not isolated. Separately training on different geometries and noise models also does not establish cross-domain generalization.

Reproducibility and limitations: Training duration is given as 200–1000 epochs without per-experiment schedules or model-selection criteria. Baseline configurations, circuit-noise parameters, and evaluation statistics are insufficiently detailed, and the source-code reference supplies no usable repository address. The limited circuit-level experiments—repetition codes and a distance-3 rotated memory—are useful preliminary checks, but do not establish practical fault-tolerant decoding performance. Together with the unresolved matching details and threshold uncertainty, these gaps prevent reliable acceptance.
